title: Best, Worst, and Average Case
summary: One algorithm has three complexities, and which one you quote changes the answer. How the cases differ, why input shape matters as much as input size, and when a worst-case guarantee is worth paying for.

slides.markdown:
"What's the complexity of quicksort?" has three correct answers: **O(n log n)**, **O(n log n)**, and **O(n²)** — best, average, and worst.

A complexity without a named case is an incomplete answer, and it's one of the fastest ways to look sloppy in an interview. It also hides real risk: the systems that fall over in production are usually the ones designed for the average case and then handed worst-case input.

This topic covers what the three cases mean, why the average case rests on an assumption you should state out loud, and how input *shape* — not size — moves you between them.

The three cases describe the **most favourable, typical, and least favourable input** of a given size — n stays fixed, only the arrangement changes.

- **Best case** — the luckiest input. Rarely useful on its own; mostly it tells you whether an early exit exists.
- **Average case** — the expected cost over some distribution of inputs. The most realistic number, and the shakiest, because it depends on an assumption about that distribution.
- **Worst case** — the adversarial input. The only one that's a **guarantee**, which is why it's the default in interviews and the one that matters for latency SLOs.

Note that these are orthogonal to O/Θ/Ω. You can state a tight bound on the worst case ("worst case Θ(n²)") or an upper bound on the average. Case = which input; O/Θ/Ω = which kind of bound. Mixing the two up is a common source of confused answers.

The simplest algorithm shows all three cleanly. Searching an unsorted array of n items:

| Case | Input | Comparisons | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best | target is the first element | 1 | O(1) |
| Average | target is somewhere, uniformly | ~n/2 | O(n) |
| Worst | target is last, or absent | n | O(n) |

Notice two things. First, best case is genuinely O(1) — and quoting that as "the" complexity of linear search would be indefensible.

Second, average and worst are the **same class** here, because n/2 and n differ only by a constant. That's typical: for many algorithms the average buys you nothing over the worst. It's precisely when they *diverge* — quicksort, hash tables — that the distinction starts to matter.

slides.sectionTitle: The average case hides an assumption
slides.markdown:
"Average case O(n log n)" is shorthand for **"expected cost, assuming inputs are drawn uniformly at random."** Change the distribution and the number changes.

Real data is almost never uniform:

- Log files arrive **nearly sorted** by timestamp.
- User IDs cluster; product catalogs are full of **duplicate** values.
- An attacker chooses the input on purpose.

That's why textbook quicksort with a first-element pivot is O(n log n) on random data and O(n²) on already-sorted data — a completely ordinary input in practice. The fix is to remove the assumption's dependence on the input: **randomize the pivot**, and the O(n²) case still exists but no adversary can trigger it deliberately.

When you quote an average case, name the assumption. "Average O(1) assuming keys distribute evenly across buckets" is a senior answer; bare "O(1)" is not.

slides.sectionTitle: Quoting the case that flatters you
slides.markdown:
The most common interview slip: answering with the best or average case when the interviewer wants the guarantee.

- "Hash map lookup is O(1)" — that's average. Worst case is **O(n)** when every key collides into one bucket.
- "Insertion sort is O(n)" — that's the already-sorted best case. Worst is **O(n²)**.
- "Quicksort is O(n log n)" — average. Worst is **O(n²)**.

None of those statements is false; each is incomplete in the direction that makes your solution look better, which is exactly what an interviewer is listening for.

Safe habit: **lead with the worst case, then add the average if it's meaningfully better.** "Worst case O(n²) if all keys collide, but O(1) average with a decent hash function" is complete, honest, and takes four seconds.

slides.sectionTitle: Shape matters as much as size
slides.markdown:
Two inputs of identical size n can land in different cases entirely. The shapes worth checking, every time:

- **Already sorted or reverse-sorted** — best case for insertion sort, worst case for naive quicksort, and a common real-world shape (timestamps, auto-increment IDs).
- **All identical values** — breaks naive partitioning schemes into O(n²); the reason production quicksorts use three-way partitioning.
- **Adversarial** — chosen specifically to hit your worst case.
- **Nearly sorted** — Timsort detects existing runs and finishes in O(n), which is why it's Python's and Java's default.

This is why a strong candidate asks "what does the data look like?" before choosing. Sorted-ness, duplicate density, and key distribution change the algorithm choice more often than n does.

Insertion sort, traced on the two extremes:

```python
def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key, j = a[i], i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:   # the inner loop is the whole story
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
```

**Best case — `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`:** the `while` condition fails immediately every time. The inner loop runs 0 times, so total work is n − 1 comparisons → **O(n)**.

**Worst case — `[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]`:** every element must travel to the front. Element i shifts i times, so the total is 1 + 2 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2 → **O(n²)**.

Same code, same n, 500,000x more work at n = 1000. The input arrangement is the only variable that changed.

slides.sectionTitle: When you must buy the guarantee
slides.markdown:
"Can you guarantee that?" is a follow-up with a real engineering point behind it: **averages don't bound tail latency.**

If a request fans out to 100 services and each has a 1% chance of hitting its slow path, roughly 63% of requests hit at least one slow path. Your p50 looks great and your p99 is a fire.

So the choice depends on what you're building:

| Situation | Optimise for | Typical pick |
|---|---|---|
| Batch job, throughput matters | average case | quicksort |
| Latency SLO, p99 matters | worst case | heapsort / merge sort |
| Untrusted input | worst case | randomized or collision-resistant structures |
| Real-time / safety-critical | worst case only | no amortized or average-case structures at all |

That last row is why hard-real-time systems ban dynamic arrays and hash tables outright: an O(1)-average structure with an O(n) spike can miss a deadline, and a missed deadline is a failure regardless of the average.

slides.sectionTitle: When the worst case is an attack
slides.subTitle: Algorithmic complexity attacks
slides.markdown:
If an attacker controls your input, your worst case becomes their tool.

**Hash-collision DoS** is the classic: a hash table degrades to O(n) per lookup when every key lands in one bucket. In 2011 researchers showed that a single crafted POST body with a few thousand colliding parameter names could pin a web server's CPU for minutes — it hit PHP, Java, Python, Ruby, and Node at once. The fix that shipped everywhere was **hash randomization**: seed the hash function per process so an attacker can't precompute collisions.

**ReDoS** is the same idea in regex form: a pattern like `(a+)+$` backtracks exponentially on a crafted string, and one request pegs a core.

The general rule: **any input-dependent worst case reachable from the network is a denial-of-service vector.** When you design with an average-case structure, ask who controls the input — that single question is what turns this topic from theory into a security review comment.

A complete answer names the case, the bound, and the trigger:

> *"Worst case O(n²), when the pivot is always the min or max — an already-sorted array does it. Average is O(n log n), and with a randomized pivot the bad case can't be triggered deliberately, though it's still possible."*

Three parts: **the number, the case, the input that causes it.** Naming the triggering input is what separates memorization from understanding — anyone can recite that quicksort is O(n²) in the worst case; knowing that sorted input triggers it means you'd catch it in a code review.

And when the cases coincide, say so — "merge sort is Θ(n log n) in all cases" is itself a selling point, and it's the reason merge sort survives in places where quicksort's average speed isn't worth its tail.
